skills.name: Astronomy
skills.description: From your cosmic address to the edge of the observable universe — the flagship 1–100 tree.

concepts.title: Andromeda, our big neighbor
concepts.description: Andromeda is the nearest large spiral galaxy, about 2.5 million light-years away.

concepts.title: Asterisms: patterns within constellations
concepts.description: Familiar star patterns like the Big Dipper are asterisms, not official constellations.

concepts.title: Stars that never set
concepts.description: Stars close to the celestial pole circle it and, from mid-northern latitudes, never dip below the horizon.

concepts.title: Constellation stars aren’t neighbors
concepts.description: Stars in the same constellation are usually at very different distances and only line up from our viewpoint.

concepts.title: What constellations are
concepts.description: Constellations are patterns of stars and, officially, 88 regions that together cover the whole sky.

concepts.title: A year is one orbit
concepts.description: Earth takes about 365.25 days to orbit the Sun once, moving at about 30 km per second.

concepts.title: Earth’s spin makes day and night
concepts.description: Earth rotates on its axis about once every 24 hours; the side facing the Sun has day.

concepts.title: Earth is the third planet
concepts.description: Our solar system has eight planets; Earth is the third from the Sun.

concepts.title: The 400× coincidence
concepts.description: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and about 400 times farther away, so they look the same size.

concepts.title: Solar vs lunar eclipses
concepts.description: A solar eclipse is the Moon blocking the Sun; a lunar eclipse is Earth's shadow falling on the Moon.

concepts.title: The ecliptic
concepts.description: The Sun’s yearly path across the sky; the Moon and planets stay close to it because the solar system is flat.

concepts.title: Gas giants and ice giants
concepts.description: Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants; Uranus and Neptune are ice giants.

concepts.title: Jupiter outweighs every other planet combined
concepts.description: Jupiter is the largest planet and has more than twice the mass of all the others put together.

concepts.title: Why leap years exist
concepts.description: The extra quarter-day in each orbit adds up, so the calendar adds a day about every four years.

concepts.title: A light-year is a distance
concepts.description: A light-year is how far light travels in a year: about 9.46 trillion km.

concepts.title: Lunar craters
concepts.description: The Moon’s craters were blasted out by impacts and survive for billions of years because the Moon has no air, water or plate tectonics to erase them.

concepts.title: The Moon’s dark “seas”
concepts.description: The dark patches on the Moon are maria: huge plains of ancient solidified lava, not water.

concepts.title: Why Mars is red
concepts.description: Mars looks red because iron oxide — rust — coats its dust and rocks.

concepts.title: The Milky Way is our galaxy
concepts.description: The Sun is one of more than a hundred billion stars in the Milky Way, a barred spiral galaxy.

concepts.title: The Milky Way is ~100,000 light-years across
concepts.description: Our galaxy is about 100,000 light-years from edge to edge.

concepts.title: The giant-impact origin of the Moon
concepts.description: The leading explanation is that the Moon formed from debris after a Mars-sized body struck the young Earth.

concepts.title: What causes Moon phases
concepts.description: Phases show how much of the Moon's sunlit half faces us; the cycle takes about 29.5 days.

concepts.title: Evidence from Moon rocks
concepts.description: Moon rocks are chemically very similar to Earth’s mantle and the Moon has only a small iron core, consistent with the giant impact.

concepts.title: The Moon always shows us the same face
concepts.description: The Moon is tidally locked: it rotates once per orbit, so the same side always faces Earth.

concepts.title: The nearest star after the Sun
concepts.description: Proxima Centauri, about 4.2 light-years away, is the closest star to the Sun.

concepts.title: The night sky changes with the seasons
concepts.description: As Earth orbits the Sun, the night side faces different directions in space, so different constellations are visible in different seasons.

concepts.title: Planets wander against the stars
concepts.description: Planets shift position against the background stars from night to night; “planet” comes from the Greek for wanderer.

concepts.title: The North Star marks north
concepts.description: Polaris sits almost directly above Earth’s North Pole, so it barely moves and marks north.

concepts.title: Earth’s wobble changes the pole star
concepts.description: Earth’s axis slowly wobbles over about 26,000 years, so the pole star changes over millennia.

concepts.title: Retrograde motion
concepts.description: Planets sometimes appear to move backwards against the stars because Earth overtakes or is overtaken by them.

concepts.title: The four rocky planets
concepts.description: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are the small, rocky inner planets.

concepts.title: Saturn's rings are ice
concepts.description: Saturn's rings are made mostly of chunks of water ice, with some rock.

concepts.title: Seasons aren't about distance
concepts.description: Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January — northern winter.

concepts.title: Seasons come from Earth's tilt
concepts.description: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°, so each hemisphere takes turns leaning toward the Sun.

concepts.title: Every sky motion has a cause
concepts.description: Daily motion comes from Earth’s spin, yearly changes from Earth’s orbit, and the Moon’s motion and gravity drive phases, eclipses and tides.

concepts.title: Why everything rises in the east
concepts.description: Earth spins west to east, so the Sun, Moon, planets and stars appear to rise in the east and set in the west.

concepts.title: Spring and neap tides
concepts.description: When the Sun and Moon line up tides are larger (spring); at right angles they are smaller (neap).

concepts.title: A star's color is its temperature
concepts.description: Blue stars are the hottest; red stars are the coolest.

concepts.title: Stars are born, age and die
concepts.description: Stars form in clouds of gas and dust. The Sun will swell into a red giant and end as a white dwarf; massive stars can explode as supernovae.

concepts.title: The Sun is about 4.6 billion years old
concepts.description: The Sun formed roughly 4.6 billion years ago.

concepts.title: The Sun runs on nuclear fusion
concepts.description: In its core the Sun fuses hydrogen into helium, releasing the energy that becomes sunlight.

concepts.title: The Sun is a star
concepts.description: The Sun is an ordinary star — the closest one to Earth — not a special category of object.

concepts.title: The Sun holds almost all the mass
concepts.description: About 99.8% of the solar system's mass is in the Sun.

concepts.title: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth
concepts.description: Light from the Sun takes roughly eight minutes to cross the distance to Earth, so we always see the Sun slightly in the past.

concepts.title: The Moon drives the tides
concepts.description: The Moon’s gravity pulls Earth’s oceans into two bulges, so most coasts get two high tides a day.

concepts.title: Billions of galaxies, 13.8 billion years
concepts.description: The observable universe holds billions of galaxies and is about 13.8 billion years old.

concepts.title: Venus is the hottest planet
concepts.description: Venus is hotter than Mercury because its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat.

levels.title: Your Cosmic Address
levels.objective: After this level you can state Earth's address: third planet from the Sun, a star in the Milky Way.
levels.summary: The Sun is a star, Earth is planet three, and our whole solar system lives in the Milky Way.

cards.headline: Every star you see at night is a sun. Ours is just the closest one.
cards.body: The Sun isn't a special kind of object. It's a star — the nearest one to Earth. The others only look like dots because they're unimaginably farther away.

cards.headline: Your address, zoomed out
cards.body: Start with Earth. It's the third of eight planets orbiting the Sun. The Sun and everything orbiting it make up our solar system.
cards.callout: Earth → planet 3 → the Sun's solar system

cards.fact: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth.
cards.context: So when you look at the Sun (please don't, directly), you're seeing it as it was roughly eight minutes ago.

cards.headline: Now zoom out much, much further
cards.body: The Sun is one of at least 100 billion stars in the Milky Way, a barred spiral galaxy. That faint band across a dark sky? That's our own galaxy, seen from the inside.

cards.headline: Cosmic address: unlocked

levels.title: The Sun, Up Close
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what powers the Sun and how dominant it is in the solar system.
levels.summary: The Sun fuses hydrogen into helium, holds 99.8% of the solar system's mass, and is about 4.6 billion years old.

cards.headline: The Sun isn't on fire. It's doing something far stranger.
cards.body: There's no burning in the everyday sense. Deep in its core, the Sun squeezes atoms together.

cards.headline: Nuclear fusion
cards.body: At about 15 million °C, the Sun's core squeezes hydrogen atoms so hard that they fuse into helium. Each fusion releases a little energy, and trillions of them every second add up to the sunlight that reaches you.

cards.fact: The Sun holds about 99.8% of the solar system's mass.
cards.context: Every planet, moon, asteroid and comet together makes up the remaining 0.2%. We're the crumbs.

cards.headline: Middle-aged, not old
cards.body: The Sun formed about 4.6 billion years ago. That sounds ancient, but for a star like ours it's roughly the middle of its life. There's plenty of hydrogen left in its core to keep the fusion going for billions of years more.

cards.headline: Sun: understood
learned: Fusion turns hydrogen into helium in the core
The core is about 15 million °C
The Sun is 99.8% of the solar system's mass
It's about 4.6 billion years old

options.rationale: There's no combustion — the Sun has no oxygen fire.

options.label: Heat left over from its formation
options.rationale: Leftover heat would have run out long ago.

options.label: Reflected light from other stars
options.rationale: The Sun makes its own light.

questions.explanation: In its core, the Sun fuses hydrogen into helium, releasing enormous energy.

questions.prompt: Why is it misleading to say the Sun is "on fire"?

options.label: Its energy comes from atoms fusing in its core, not burning
It's actually cold on the inside
options.rationale: The core is about 15 million °C.

options.label: It only reflects light from other stars
options.rationale: The Sun makes its own light.

options.label: It has no fuel left
options.rationale: It has billions of years of hydrogen left.

questions.explanation: Fire is a chemical reaction that needs oxygen. The Sun's energy comes from nuclear fusion: hydrogen atoms fusing into helium under enormous heat and pressure.

options.rationale: Planets don't make their own light.

options.label: A galaxy
options.rationale: A galaxy contains billions of stars.

options.label: A nebula
options.rationale: A nebula is a cloud of gas and dust.

questions.explanation: The Sun is a star — the closest one to Earth.

levels.title: The Rocky Four
levels.objective: After this level you can name the rocky planets and explain why Venus, not Mercury, is the hottest.
levels.summary: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are rocky. Venus is the hottest planet thanks to its heat-trapping atmosphere, and Mars is red because of rust.

cards.headline: Mercury is closest to the Sun. So why is Venus hotter?
The inner planets are rocky
cards.body: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are small worlds of rock and metal. You could, in principle, stand on any of them. You wouldn't enjoy most of them.

cards.headline: Venus: a runaway greenhouse
cards.body: Venus is wrapped in a thick carbon dioxide atmosphere that traps heat. Its surface is over 450 °C — hotter than Mercury, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun.

cards.fact: Mars is red because it's rusty.
cards.context: Iron oxide (the same stuff as rust) coats Martian dust and rocks, and fine red dust in its thin atmosphere tints the whole planet.

cards.headline: Inner solar system: mapped
learned: Four rocky planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars

Its CO₂ atmosphere traps heat
Mars gets its red color from iron oxide

questions.explanation: The rocky inner planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars. Jupiter is a gas giant.

levels.title: Giants of the Outer Dark
levels.objective: After this level you can tell gas giants from ice giants and describe Jupiter's and Saturn's standout features.
levels.summary: Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants, Uranus and Neptune are ice giants. Jupiter outweighs every other planet combined, and Saturn's rings are mostly ice.

cards.headline: Past Mars, the planets stop being rocky and start being enormous.

items.label: Gas giants

items.label: Ice giants

cards.headline: Saturn's rings are ice
cards.body: Those famous rings aren't solid. They're countless chunks of water ice, with some rock, ranging from dust-sized grains to pieces as big as houses. Each chunk orbits Saturn on its own path, like a tiny moon.

levels.title: Why We Have Seasons
levels.objective: After this level you can explain that seasons come from Earth's tilt, not its distance from the Sun.
levels.summary: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°. Each hemisphere takes turns leaning toward the Sun, which is why seasons are opposite north and south.

cards.headline: Most people get this one wrong: summer isn't when Earth is closest to the Sun.

cards.fact: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January.
cards.context: That's the middle of winter in the Northern Hemisphere. So distance can't be what makes summer.

cards.headline: It's the tilt
cards.body: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°. When your hemisphere leans toward the Sun, sunlight hits the ground more directly and days last longer, so more energy lands on each patch of ground. That's summer. Lean away, and the same sunlight arrives at a slant and spreads thin.

cards.headline: Opposite seasons
cards.body: Because the hemispheres lean opposite ways, December is winter in New York and summer in Sydney. Same planet, same distance, different lean.

cards.headline: Seasons: solved
learned: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°
Tilt, not distance, causes seasons
Earth is closest to the Sun in January
The hemispheres have opposite seasons

options.label: Changes in the Sun's brightness

options.label: The Moon's position

questions.explanation: Earth's ~23.5° tilt changes how directly sunlight hits each hemisphere through the year.

questions.explanation: Venus's atmosphere traps heat, and Earth's tilt sets the angle of sunlight. In both cases something other than distance is in charge.

levels.title: The Moon's Changing Face
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Moon phases and why we only ever see one side of the Moon.
levels.summary: Phases show how much of the Moon's sunlit half faces us, over a ~29.5-day cycle. The Moon is tidally locked, so the same side always faces Earth.

cards.headline: The Moon doesn't change shape. You're just seeing it from a different angle.
Half lit, always
cards.body: The Sun always lights up half of the Moon. As the Moon orbits Earth, we see different amounts of that lit half: a thin crescent, a half, the full face, then back again. Nothing is covering the Moon; only our viewing angle changes.
cards.callout: A full cycle takes about 29.5 days

cards.fact: We always see the same side of the Moon.
cards.context: The Moon, about 384,400 km away, is tidally locked: it turns exactly once per orbit. The far side isn't permanently dark. It gets as much sunlight as the near side; we just never see it from Earth. Its day and its month last the same time.

cards.headline: Moon: decoded
learned: Phases = how much of the lit half we see
A full phase cycle takes about 29.5 days
The Moon is tidally locked

levels.title: Eclipses and a Cosmic Coincidence
levels.objective: After this level you can tell solar from lunar eclipses and explain why the Moon can exactly cover the Sun.
levels.summary: A solar eclipse is the Moon blocking the Sun; a lunar eclipse is Earth's shadow on the Moon. The Sun is ~400× wider and ~400× farther than the Moon.

cards.headline: By pure luck, the Moon is exactly the right size to blot out the Sun.

items.label: Solar eclipse
points: The Moon passes between the Sun and Earth
The Moon's shadow falls on Earth

items.label: Lunar eclipse
points: Earth passes between the Sun and Moon
Earth's shadow falls on the Moon

cards.fact: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon — and about 400 times farther away.
cards.context: Those two numbers cancel out, so the Sun and Moon look almost exactly the same size in our sky. That's why, during a total solar eclipse, the Moon can cover the Sun's bright disc and reveal its faint outer glow.

cards.headline: Eclipses: explained
learned: Solar eclipse: the Moon blocks the Sun
Lunar eclipse: Earth's shadow falls on the Moon
The 400× coincidence makes total solar eclipses possible

questions.explanation: At full Moon, Earth is between the Sun and the Moon. When the three line up exactly, Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.

levels.title: Light-Years: Measuring the Unmeasurable
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what a light-year measures and how far the nearest star is.
levels.summary: A light-year is a distance — about 9.46 trillion km. The nearest star after the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.2 light-years away.

cards.headline: A light-year sounds like a unit of time. It isn't.
Distance, measured in light
cards.body: A light-year is how far light travels in one year: about 9.46 trillion kilometers. Astronomers use it because kilometers stop being useful very quickly.

cards.headline: Why measure space in light?
cards.body: Light is the fastest thing there is, about 300,000 km every second. It crosses from the Moon to Earth in just over a second. Yet even light needs years to reach the next star, so astronomers describe distance by how long light takes to cover it.

cards.fact: The closest star after the Sun is Proxima Centauri, about 4.2 light-years away.
cards.context: Its light left before you started reading about this app. Probably.

levels.title: The Life of a Star
levels.objective: After this level you can read a star's temperature from its color and outline how the Sun will end.
levels.summary: Stars are born in clouds of gas and dust. Blue stars are hottest, red coolest. The Sun will become a red giant and then a white dwarf; massive stars can go supernova.

cards.headline: Stars have a life story: birth, a long middle age, and a very dramatic ending.
Color is temperature
cards.body: Look closely and stars have colors. Blue-white stars are the hottest; red stars are the coolest. The Sun sits in between, which is why it looks white-yellow.

events.label: Forms from a collapsing cloud of gas and dust
Fusing hydrogen into helium in its core
Sheds its outer layers and ends as a white dwarf

cards.headline: Bigger stars, bigger endings
cards.body: The Sun won't explode. But stars much more massive than the Sun can end their lives in a supernova — an explosion that can briefly outshine a whole galaxy.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Your Place in the Universe
levels.objective: After this level you can trace Earth's address from our planet all the way out to the observable universe.
levels.summary: The Milky Way is ~100,000 light-years across, Andromeda is ~2.5 million light-years away, and the observable universe holds billions of galaxies in a ~13.8-billion-year-old cosmos.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 finale. Let's zoom all the way out.
cards.body: Everything from Levels 1–9 was your neighborhood. Now for the city, the country and the planet.

cards.headline: Our galaxy
cards.body: The Milky Way is about 100,000 light-years across. Light from one edge would take 100,000 years to reach the other.

cards.fact: Andromeda, the nearest large spiral galaxy, is about 2.5 million light-years away.
cards.context: On a dark night you can see it with the naked eye as a faint smudge — the most distant thing most people will ever see unaided.

cards.headline: And then everything else
cards.body: The observable universe holds billions of galaxies, each with billions of stars. The universe itself is about 13.8 billion years old.

levels.title: Why the Sky Turns
levels.objective: After this level you can explain that day and night, and the stars rising and setting, come from Earth spinning.
levels.summary: Earth spins once a day from west to east, so the Sun and stars appear to rise in the east and set in the west.

cards.headline: The sky isn’t turning. You are.
cards.body: Every sunrise is really your patch of Earth rolling toward the Sun. Stay up all night and you’ll see the stars do exactly the same thing.

cards.headline: One spin, one day
cards.body: Earth spins around its axis, an imaginary line through the North and South Poles, about once every 24 hours. The half facing the Sun has day; the half facing away has night. As Earth turns, you’re carried from one half into the other.

cards.headline: Why everything rises in the east
cards.body: Earth spins from west to east. That turns your eastern horizon toward the Sun first, so the Sun seems to climb up in the east and sink in the west. The Moon, the planets and the stars cross the sky the same way, for the same reason.

cards.fact: At the equator, Earth’s surface moves at about 1,670 km/h.
cards.context: You don’t feel it because you, the ground and the air all move together at a steady speed.

cards.headline: Daily spin: understood
learned: Earth spins once about every 24 hours
Day is the half of Earth facing the Sun
Earth spins from west to east
So the Sun, Moon and stars rise in the east

options.label: The Sun circling Earth
options.rationale: It looks that way, but it’s Earth that turns.

options.label: Earth orbiting the Sun
options.rationale: That takes a whole year, not a day.

options.label: The Moon blocking the Sun
options.rationale: That’s an eclipse, and it’s rare.

questions.explanation: Earth spins about once every 24 hours; the half facing the Sun has day and the other half has night.

questions.prompt: Why does the Sun rise in the east?

options.label: The Sun orbits Earth from east to west
options.rationale: Earth’s spin creates the Sun’s daily path, not an orbit of the Sun.

options.label: The east is closer to the Sun
options.rationale: Every horizon is the same distance from the Sun.

options.label: Earth spins toward the east, turning the eastern horizon to face the Sun first
Earth’s tilt points the east at the Sun

questions.explanation: Earth rotates from west to east, so your eastern horizon swings into sunlight first and the Sun appears to rise there.

options.label: Stars orbit Earth once a day
options.rationale: Stars are far beyond Earth; they don’t orbit us.

options.label: Stars are pulled by the Moon
options.rationale: The Moon doesn’t move the stars.

options.label: Earth’s spin sweeps every object in the sky across it the same way

questions.explanation: The stars aren’t moving across the sky. Earth’s west-to-east spin makes the Sun and every distant sun appear to rise in the east and set in the west.

levels.title: A Year Around the Sun
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what a year is, why leap years exist, and why the night sky changes with the seasons.
levels.summary: A year is one orbit of about 365.25 days. The quarter-days add up to leap days, and the night sky shifts as we orbit.

cards.headline: A year is just one lap.
cards.body: Every birthday, Earth has made one full trip around the Sun since the last one.

cards.headline: One lap, 940 million kilometers
cards.body: Earth takes about 365.25 days to orbit the Sun once. In that time it travels roughly 940 million km, which works out to about 30 km every second. Right now you’re moving faster than any rocket has ever launched.

cards.headline: Where the quarter-days go
cards.body: Calendars count 365 days, but each orbit takes about a quarter of a day longer. Those quarters add up to roughly one full day every four years, so we add February 29 in leap years to keep the calendar in step with the seasons.

cards.headline: A different night sky each season
cards.body: At night you face away from the Sun. As Earth moves around its orbit, that view swings toward different parts of space, so each season has its own constellations. Orion, for example, is a winter evening sight in the Northern Hemisphere.

cards.headline: Orbit: understood
learned: A year is one orbit: about 365.25 days
Earth travels about 30 km every second
Leap days catch up the extra quarter-days
The night sky changes as we orbit

options.label: 24 hours
options.rationale: That’s one spin on its axis: a day.

options.label: 29.5 days
options.rationale: That’s the Moon’s cycle of phases.

options.label: 4 years
options.rationale: Leap years come every four years; the orbit takes one.

questions.explanation: One orbit of the Sun takes about 365.25 days: one year.

questions.prompt: Why do we add a leap day about every four years?

options.label: Each orbit takes about a quarter-day longer than 365 days
Earth slows down every four years
options.rationale: Earth’s orbit doesn’t change like that.

options.label: To make up for the Moon’s orbit
options.rationale: Leap days track Earth’s orbit around the Sun, not the Moon.

options.label: Because February is too short
options.rationale: February is just where the extra day goes.

questions.explanation: A year is about 365.25 days. The extra quarter-days add up to about one day every four years, so leap years add February 29.

options.label: Earth moves much closer to the Sun, then farther away
options.rationale: Distance isn’t the cause; Earth is closest in January.

options.label: The Sun gets hotter, then cooler

options.label: Earth’s tilted axis leans each hemisphere toward, then away from, the Sun
Earth spins faster in summer
options.rationale: Earth’s spin rate stays essentially the same.

questions.explanation: Earth’s axis stays tilted the same way as it orbits, so over one year each hemisphere leans toward the Sun (summer) and then away from it (winter).

levels.title: Connect the Dots: Constellations
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what a constellation is and why its stars usually aren’t near each other.
levels.summary: There are 88 official constellations covering the sky. Their stars only line up from our viewpoint.

cards.headline: Orion isn’t really a hunter, and his stars aren’t even neighbors.
cards.body: Constellations are patterns we see from one spot in space: Earth.

cards.headline: Patterns and regions
cards.body: People have long named star patterns after figures, animals and objects. Today astronomers use 88 official constellations. Each one is a region of sky with set boundaries, like countries on a map, and together they cover the whole sky.

cards.headline: A trick of perspective
cards.body: Stars that look side by side can be wildly different distances away. One might be a few dozen light-years from us, its neighbor in the pattern hundreds. From anywhere else in the galaxy, the same stars would make completely different shapes.

cards.fact: The Big Dipper is not a constellation.
cards.context: It’s an asterism: a familiar pattern inside the constellation Ursa Major, the Great Bear.

cards.headline: Constellations: decoded

There are 88 official constellations
Their stars are usually far apart in space

questions.prompt: How many official constellations are there?

options.rationale: That’s the number of zodiac signs; the constellations cover the whole sky.

questions.explanation: Astronomers officially recognize 88 constellations, which together cover the entire sky.

questions.explanation: A constellation is a pattern seen from Earth. Stars in it can be at very different distances and just happen to line up from our viewpoint.

options.label: Their light reaches us at the same moment it leaves

questions.explanation: A light-year is how far light travels in a year. Light from a star 500 light-years away left it about 500 years ago; from 50 light-years, about 50 years ago.

levels.title: The North Star
levels.objective: After this level you can find north with Polaris and explain why some stars never set.
levels.summary: Polaris sits above the North Pole, so it stays put while the sky wheels around it. Its height gives your latitude.

cards.headline: One star barely moves all night. It has guided travelers for centuries.
The star above the pole
cards.body: Polaris, the North Star, lies almost directly above Earth’s North Pole. As Earth spins, every other star circles around it while Polaris stays nearly fixed, marking north. It isn’t the brightest star, either: that’s Sirius.

cards.headline: Stars that never set
cards.body: From mid-northern latitudes, stars close to Polaris trace small circles around it and never dip below the horizon. They’re called circumpolar stars. Bonus: Polaris’s height above your horizon, in degrees, roughly equals your latitude.

cards.fact: Polaris won’t be the North Star forever.
cards.context: Earth’s axis slowly wobbles, tracing a circle about every 26,000 years, so the pole points at different stars over the ages. The Southern Hemisphere has no bright pole star at all; navigators there use the Southern Cross to find south.

cards.headline: North: found
learned: Polaris sits almost directly above the North Pole
It marks north; its height gives your latitude
Circumpolar stars never set

options.label: It orbits Earth at the same speed Earth spins
options.rationale: Stars don’t orbit Earth.

options.label: You are in the Southern Hemisphere

options.rationale: Its height in the sky shows your latitude, not its distance.

options.label: It is 4 o’clock
options.rationale: Polaris stays put all night, so it can’t tell the time.

options.label: You are at roughly 40° north latitude

questions.explanation: In the Northern Hemisphere, Polaris’s height above the horizon in degrees roughly equals your latitude.

questions.prompt: From Level 11: most stars rise in the east and set in the west. Why don’t the circumpolar stars set?

questions.explanation: Earth’s spin makes every star appear to circle the pole. Stars close to Polaris trace circles small enough to stay above the horizon all night.

levels.title: The Ecliptic: The Planets’ Highway
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why the Sun, Moon and planets all travel along the same narrow band of sky.
levels.summary: The ecliptic is the Sun’s yearly path. The Moon and planets stay near it because the solar system is flat.

cards.headline: The planets don’t roam the whole sky. They stick to one narrow road.
The Sun’s yearly path
cards.body: As Earth orbits, the Sun seems to drift slowly against the background stars, returning to the same spot after a year. The line it traces is called the ecliptic. The constellations it passes through are the zodiac constellations.
cards.callout: Ecliptic = the Sun’s path over a year

cards.headline: A flat solar system
cards.body: The planets all orbit the Sun in nearly the same flat plane, and the Moon orbits Earth close to it too. Seen from inside that plane, we see everything strung along one line: the ecliptic. Spot a bright “star” near where the Sun set? Check if it’s a planet.

cards.fact: Eclipses can only happen when the Moon is on the ecliptic.
cards.context: The Moon’s orbit is tilted slightly, so most months it passes just above or below the Sun’s path. Only when it crosses the ecliptic at the right moment do we get an eclipse.

cards.headline: Planetary highway: mapped
learned: The ecliptic is the Sun’s path over a year

Eclipses need the Moon on the ecliptic

options.label: The path of the Moon’s shadow

options.label: The path the Sun appears to follow across the sky over a year

options.rationale: The ecliptic is set by Earth’s orbit.

options.label: They are pulled toward the Sun’s path by the stars
options.rationale: Distant stars have no such effect.

options.label: Their orbits lie in nearly the same flat plane as Earth’s

questions.explanation: The solar system is flat: the planets orbit in nearly the same plane as Earth, so from Earth they all appear close to the Sun’s path.

options.label: The Moon is too small most months

options.label: The Moon usually passes just above or below the Sun’s path

questions.explanation: The Moon’s orbit is slightly tilted to the ecliptic. Most new Moons pass above or below the Sun; only a line-up on the ecliptic gives a solar eclipse.

levels.title: Wanderers: How Planets Move Across the Sky
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why planets drift against the stars and sometimes appear to loop backwards.
levels.summary: Planets drift against the stars as they orbit. When Earth overtakes an outer planet, it seems to go backwards: retrograde motion.

cards.headline: Every few years, Mars seems to stop, reverse and loop back across the sky.
cards.body: It never actually turns around. You’re watching from a moving planet.

cards.headline: The wanderers
cards.body: Night after night, the stars keep the same patterns. Planets don’t: they slowly shift position against the background stars as they orbit the Sun. The ancient Greeks noticed, and the word “planet” comes from their word for “wanderer.”

cards.headline: Overtaking on the inside lane
cards.body: Earth orbits closer to the Sun than Mars does, so it moves faster. When Earth catches up with Mars and passes it, Mars appears to slide backwards against the stars for a few weeks, then forward again. It’s like passing a slower car: it seems to drift backwards, though both are going forward.

cards.context: No planet ever reverses direction in its orbit. The backwards loop is a change in our viewpoint, not in the planet’s path.

cards.headline: Wanderers: explained
learned: Planets drift against the stars as they orbit
“Planet” means wanderer
Earth overtaking Mars makes it seem to go backwards
Retrograde motion is only apparent

options.label: Child of the Sun

questions.explanation: Planets drift against the fixed patterns of stars, so the Greeks called them “wanderers.”

options.label: Earth

questions.explanation: Mars is the rocky planet just outside Earth’s orbit. Earth overtakes it every couple of years, causing its retrograde loop.

levels.title: Tides: The Moon’s Pull on the Ocean
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why most coasts get two high tides a day and what spring and neap tides are.
levels.summary: The Moon’s gravity makes two bulges of ocean water. Earth spins through both each day; the Sun makes tides bigger or smaller.

cards.headline: The Moon moves oceans. Twice a day.
Two bulges, not one
cards.body: The Moon’s gravity pulls on Earth’s oceans, stretching them into two bulges: one facing the Moon and one on the opposite side of Earth. As Earth spins, most coastlines pass through both bulges, getting two high tides and two low tides about every 24 hours and 50 minutes.

cards.headline: The Sun joins in
cards.body: The Sun pulls on the oceans too, more weakly. Around new and full Moon, the Sun, Moon and Earth line up and their pulls combine into extra-high and extra-low tides: spring tides. Around the quarter Moons they pull at right angles and tides are gentler: neap tides.

cards.fact: Spring tides have nothing to do with spring.
cards.context: They happen twice a month, all year round. The name comes from water “springing” up higher.

options.label: Earth’s tilt

options.label: The Sun’s heat

questions.explanation: Tides come mainly from the Moon’s gravity, with a smaller pull from the Sun.

levels.title: Where the Moon Came From
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the giant-impact explanation for the Moon’s origin and the evidence for it.
levels.summary: The Moon most likely formed from debris after a Mars-sized body hit the young Earth about 4.5 billion years ago.

cards.headline: The Moon may be made of pieces of Earth.
cards.body: The leading explanation starts with one of the biggest collisions in the solar system’s history.

cards.headline: The giant impact
cards.body: About 4.5 billion years ago, soon after Earth formed, a Mars-sized body (scientists call it Theia) is thought to have slammed into it. The crash threw huge amounts of molten rock into orbit, and that debris gathered to form the Moon.

cards.headline: The clues
cards.body: Rocks brought back by Apollo astronauts are chemically very similar to rocks from Earth’s mantle, the layer below the crust. And the Moon has only a small iron core, which fits a Moon built mostly from rocky outer layers rather than Earth’s iron heart. Computer simulations of such a collision can produce exactly this kind of Moon.

cards.headline: Moon origin: reconstructed
learned: The Moon likely formed from a giant impact
A Mars-sized body (Theia) hit the young Earth
That was about 4.5 billion years ago

options.label: It split off from Mars

questions.explanation: A Mars-sized body likely hit the young Earth, and the Moon formed from the debris.

levels.title: Craters and Seas on the Moon
levels.objective: After this level you can explain where lunar craters and the dark “seas” came from and why they last so long.
levels.summary: Craters are impact scars preserved for billions of years; the dark maria are ancient hardened lava.

cards.headline: The “Man in the Moon” is made of ancient lava.
Scars that never heal
cards.body: The Moon’s craters were blasted out by asteroids and comets, and range from tiny pits to basins hundreds of kilometers wide. On Earth, wind, rain and shifting plates wear craters away. The Moon has almost no atmosphere, no liquid water and no plate tectonics, so its craters survive for billions of years.
cards.callout: No air, no water, no erasing

cards.headline: Seas without water
cards.body: The dark patches are called maria, Latin for “seas,” because early astronomers thought they might be water. They’re actually vast plains of ancient lava that flooded low areas and hardened. Most of them are on the near side, the side that faces Earth.

cards.headline: Lunar surface: surveyed
learned: Craters come from asteroid and comet impacts
No air, water or plate tectonics erase them
Maria are plains of ancient hardened lava
Most maria are on the near side

questions.prompt: What are the dark patches on the Moon, called maria?

options.label: Oceans of water
options.rationale: The name means “seas,” but they’re dry.

options.label: Shadows of mountains
options.rationale: The patches are dark rock, not shadows.

options.label: Areas the Sun never lights
options.rationale: Sunlight reaches them like the rest of the surface.

questions.explanation: The maria are enormous plains of lava that erupted and hardened long ago.

questions.prompt: Why do craters last so much longer on the Moon than on Earth?

options.label: The Moon is hit less often
options.rationale: It’s more that nothing erases the craters.

options.label: The Moon has no weather, water or plate tectonics to erase them
Moon rock is harder than Earth rock
options.rationale: The difference is what wears craters away.

options.label: The Moon’s gravity is stronger
options.rationale: The Moon’s gravity is weaker than Earth’s.

questions.explanation: Wind, water and moving plates wear down Earth’s craters. The Moon has none of these, so its craters survive for billions of years.

questions.prompt: From Level 6: why can we see most of the Moon’s maria from Earth?

options.label: The maria reflect the most sunlight
options.rationale: They’re actually darker than the rest of the Moon.

options.label: The Moon rotates so we see all sides
options.rationale: The Moon is tidally locked; we see one side.

options.label: The far side has no surface features
options.rationale: The far side is heavily cratered.

options.label: Most maria are on the near side, which always faces Earth

questions.explanation: The Moon is tidally locked, always showing us the same face, and most of the maria are on that near side.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Reading the Sky
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the everyday motions of the Sun, Moon, stars and planets and the tides they cause.
levels.summary: Spin makes days, orbits make years and seasons, and the Moon’s orbit and gravity drive phases, eclipses and tides.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 finale. Everything in the sky moves for a reason.
cards.body: You now know the reason for almost all of it. Let’s put it together.

cards.headline: Spin, orbit, pull
cards.body: Earth’s spin gives day and night and sweeps the stars across the sky. Its orbit gives the year, the seasons and a changing night sky. And the Moon, circling us, brings phases, eclipses and tides.
cards.callout: Spin → day · Orbit → year · Moon → tides

cards.fact: Each star rises about 4 minutes earlier every night.
cards.context: Earth moves a little along its orbit each day, so the stars get a head start. Over a year those minutes add up to a whole different night sky.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 complete
learned: Earth’s spin: day, night and a turning sky
Earth’s orbit: the year and a changing night sky
The Moon: phases, eclipses and tides
Planets wander; Mars sometimes loops backwards

questions.prompt: Which motion gives us day and night?

options.label: Earth orbiting the Sun
options.rationale: That gives us the year.

options.label: The Moon orbiting Earth
options.rationale: That gives us the Moon’s phases.

options.label: The Sun orbiting Earth
options.rationale: It’s Earth that turns.

questions.explanation: Earth’s daily spin carries each place into sunlight and then into darkness.

questions.prompt: Which star stays almost fixed above the North Pole?

options.label: Sirius
options.rationale: Sirius is the brightest night-time star, not the pole star.

options.label: Proxima Centauri
options.rationale: That’s the nearest star, far from the pole in our sky.

options.label: The Sun
options.rationale: The Sun rises and sets.

questions.explanation: Polaris lies almost directly above Earth’s North Pole, so it barely moves.

questions.prompt: Why does the night sky show different constellations in different seasons?

options.label: The stars move to new positions
options.rationale: The stars’ patterns stay the same for centuries.

options.label: Earth’s tilt hides some stars
options.rationale: Tilt causes seasons, not which stars face us at night.

options.label: As Earth orbits, the night side faces different parts of space
The Moon blocks different stars each season
options.rationale: The Moon covers only a tiny patch of sky.

questions.explanation: At night we face away from the Sun. As Earth moves around its orbit, that direction changes, so different constellations are overhead.

questions.prompt: Mars appears to move backwards for a few weeks. What’s really happening?

options.label: Mars reverses in its orbit
options.rationale: Planets never reverse; it’s an illusion.

options.label: The Moon pulls Mars backwards
options.rationale: The Moon doesn’t affect Mars’s motion.

options.label: Mars is behind the Sun
options.rationale: Then we couldn’t see it at all.

options.label: Earth is overtaking Mars on its faster inner orbit

questions.explanation: Earth’s faster orbit catches up with and passes Mars, making Mars appear to slide backwards against the stars.

questions.prompt: Chapter 2 recap: which pairing of cause and effect is correct?

options.label: Earth’s tilt → tides
options.rationale: Tilt causes seasons; the Moon’s gravity causes tides.

options.label: The Moon’s gravity → day and night
options.rationale: Earth’s spin causes day and night.

options.label: Earth’s spin → stars rising in the east
Earth’s orbit → the Moon’s craters
options.rationale: Craters come from impacts.

questions.explanation: Earth spins west to east, so every star rises in the east. Tides come from the Moon’s gravity, seasons from tilt, and craters from impacts.
